content.text: Scene 1
Scene 1
(Setting: a clearing in a wooded area at night. CHIP, PA, and GETTY are sitting around a fire.)
GETTY: You've heard?
PA: Yes. Folks are saying she's angry.
GETTY: Furious.
PA: But why?

GETTY: (shrugging) Who knows? I steer well clear of Fowl. Doesn't everyone? She could destroy us in one fiery breath. But I'll tell you this. I'm restringing my bows and sharpening my arrows. Mixing up some battle potions, too.
CHIP: (shivering) Pa, I'm going to bed.
(PA nods and continues to murmur with GETTY. CHIP walks toward the cabin, sneaks a look behind him, and darts to the oak tree.)
CHIP: (whispering) Sage!
(SAGE appears in the tree.)
CHIP: There's trouble with Fowl.
SAGE: I've heard. (sighing) Perhaps…it's related to broken promises.
CHIP: Huh? You mean the Heart-Fruit Deal?
(SAGE nods.)
CHIP: But we kept our end! We left heart-fruit for her, like we do every year.
SAGE: The original deal was quite strict. The Elf Folk can live in Wingland in exchange for one hundred pieces of heart-fruit per year. (SAGE flaps her wings.) Did you give enough this season?
CHIP: Of course not, because of the drought. Everyone knows we had less heart-fruit.
SAGE: Did anyone discuss it with her?
(CHIP starts to answer, then stops.)
SAGE: The Elf Folk and the birds used to have regular meetings, you know.
CHIP: Wait, with Fowl?

SAGE: Certainly. Honest, direct talking. But the tradition died out. Elf Folk avoid Fowl's meadow entirely now, except to drop the heart-fruit and run. (sighing) They don't talk with any of us birds anymore. They used to visit me for advice, but now they think I'm just a batty old owl.
CHIP: I visit you.
SAGE: You're just a boy.
CHIP: I'm also an Elf Folk. I'll make this right.
Scene 2
Scene 2
(Setting: a meadow. CHIP is dragging the sack toward the willow trees. FOWL appears. She spreads her wings and hisses, towering over CHIP.)
CHIP: (voice shaking) I mean you no harm! I spoke with Sage!
FOWL: (lowering her wings) Sage? She is very wise.
(PA runs into the meadow with a bow and arrow. FOWL screeches and blows fire. CHIP runs between PA and FOWL, yelling and waving his arms.)
PA: (angrily, to Fowl) Leave my son alone!
CHIP: Pa! We're just talking!
PA: (lowering his bow) Talking?
(FOWL tucks her wings.)
CHIP: And I'm giving her heart-fruit; we didn't give her enough.
PA: We had a bad farming year, you know that! The plan was to give her more next season.
CHIP: But you didn't tell her that, Pa! Sage says that Elf Folk and the birds used to have meetings. Now we just ignore our problems until they're out of control.
PA: Meetings?
FOWL: (to PA) Your grandfather and I led them together. Every full moon. Moon Meeting, we called it. You were there once, but you wouldn't remember.
PA: (with a faraway look) That was real? I thought I dreamed that.
FOWL: Very real.
PA: In the dream, you…blew fire for us. Beautiful fire, with so many colors.
FOWL: (smiling slightly) It wasn't a dream.
(PA, CHIP, and FOWL stare at each other. PA picks up the sack and offers it to FOWL.)
FOWL: (lowering her head to her chest) Thank you.
PA: We'll see you at the next full moon.
FOWL: (stunned) Moon Meeting?
PA: Of course.
FOWL: I-I'll prepare my fireworks.
CHIP: And I'll tell Sage.
PA: Maybe she'll have advice on how to hurry the rain.

contents.text: In Scene 1, an Elf Folk boy named Chip learns that the reason that Fowl, a fire-breathing bird, and the Elf Folk don't get along is that they don't talk about things the way they used to.
In Scene 2, Chip sets out to talk to Fowl so that Fowl and the Elf Folk can communicate again.
So, the play is about an Elf Folk boy who tries to fix the troubled relationship between his people and a fire-breathing bird.

content.text: Scene 1
Scene 1
(Setting: Snidely's Bake Shop, many years ago. SNIDELY is waiting on the MYSTERIOUS CUSTOMER, her face hidden by her hooded cloak.)
MYSTERIOUS CUSTOMER: I heard you might bake the best muffins in the land. Would you accept this magic mirror in exchange for some?
SNIDELY: (annoyed) What do you mean I might bake the best muffins?
MYSTERIOUS CUSTOMER: Well…I asked the mirror to direct me to the best chef in the land. But it couldn't decide between you and Chef Bertha.
SNIDELY: (furious) Bertha? Seriously? Give me that mirror. I'll ask it myself!
MYSTERIOUS CUSTOMER: Only the mirror's owner may ask the questions. I'll trade it for a dozen muffins.
SNIDELY: Fine!
(SNIDELY gives the MYSTERIOUS CUSTOMER the muffins and snatches the mirror. The MYSTERIOUS CUSTOMER hurries out.)
SNIDELY: Okay, mirror. Who's the best chef in the land?
(The mirror lights up.)
MIRROR: That's a tough one. It's either you or Chef Bertha.
(SNIDELY shakes the mirror.)

content.text: (to SNIDELY)

pieces.text: Your pudding is my favorite dessert, you know.
SNIDELY:

content.text: (chest puffed)

pieces.text: Took me a year to perfect that dish.

contents.text: At the beginning of the play, Snidely wants to be told he is the best chef in the land. He is focused on his own talent and does not recognize Bertha's talent. By the end, he has realized that he and Bertha excel at different dishes. He no longer feels the need to be seen as the best chef in the land.
So, from these clues, you can guess that Snidely has become less self-centered and more open-minded.

content.text: Scene 1
Scene 1
(Setting: the kitchen. JANA is chopping carrots as AUNTIE TIMIKA stirs the pot.)
AUNTIE TIMIKA: How's your comic book coming along? Do you have a new superhero?
JANA: Actually, I came up with three superheroes! They're based on some kids in my class.
AUNTIE TIMIKA: Really? New friends?
(JANA picks up her sketchbook from the table to show AUNTIE TIMIKA.)

JANA: (with an embarrassed laugh) Well, not exactly friends, since I don't have the guts to actually talk to any of them. But they're really cool. This is Super Keisha. Her superpower is having an amazing singing voice. And this is Super Hal, whose superpower is being an awesome dancer. Super Tessa tells great jokes.
AUNTIE TIMIKA: (studying the pictures) These are great! You should put yourself in the story, too.
JANA: (frowning) Yeah, no. I have exactly zero superpowers.
AUNTIE TIMIKA: That's not—
(JANA's phone rings. She looks at the screen, eyebrows scrunched.)
JANA: Strange. It's this new boy, Rupert. Ms. Barrington made us study partners, but we never call each other.
AUNTIE TIMIKA: Well, he's calling now. Answer it!
JANA: (into the phone) Uh…hi? Well…sure, I…guess. Uh…okay, bye.
(JANA ends the call, her expression stunned.)
AUNTIE TIMIKA: Well?
JANA: (anxiously) He invited me to his birthday party, and I said yes. But only because I felt stuck. Ugh! I never know what to say at parties.
AUNTIE TIMIKA: If you said yes, you need to show up. Who knows? Maybe you'll have fun.
JANA: I seriously doubt it.
Scene 2
Scene 2

(Setting: a backyard, decorated for a birthday party. KEISHA, HAL, TESSA, and RUPERT are at the table eating snacks, laughing, and talking. JANA sits at the same table but is off to the side, looking through her sketchbook.)
RUPERT: I'm telling you, I've read Secrets of the Powdery Forest like ten times. Princess Fangs bites Swan Man, and he loses the power of flight. Don't you remember?
(JANA perks up, closing her sketchbook.)
TESSA: Nope, because it's Leaf Girl who lost the power of flight. Not Swan Man.
(JANA opens her mouth to speak, but KEISHA talks first.)
KEISHA: They both lost the power of flight.
(JANA opens her mouth again, but HAL talks first.)
HAL: Nobody lost the power of flight! They—

JANA: (blurting) Actually, Princess Fangs bit Swan Man in Night Cave. That's when he lost the power of flight. Princess Fangs almost bit Leaf Girl in Terrible Twilight, but Uncle Wind stopped her. Look, I drew pictures of it.
(JANA opens her sketchbook to show the others.)
RUPERT: (studying the pictures and laughing) She's right. We're all busted.
KEISHA: I remember these scenes now. Wow, you can really draw!
(The others nod.)
KEISHA: Can we see more?
JANA: Uh, I guess… (She turns the page, then freezes in alarm.) Wait, not this one—
RUPERT: Is that Hal?
Hal: (leaning in) Whoa! I'm a dancing superhero!
KEISHA: Am I in there?
TESSA: Am I?
JANA: (turning the page uncertainly) Yeah. I hope you don't mind.
KEISHA: Hey, I'm a singing superhero!
TESSA: And I'm a performing superhero. These are amazing.
RUPERT: Can you do me as a basketball superhero?
(JANA nods, smiling.)
RUPERT: Is your picture in here?
JANA: Me? No way.
KEISHA: Are you kidding? You should draw yourself as a comic artist superhero.
HAL: You could sell these!
TESSA: Definitely. Why'd you keep your comics a secret?
JANA: (grinning, pleased by the compliments) I don't know. Maybe I just…needed a superhero shove.

content.text: play

pieces.text: is a story that is written so it can be performed for an audience. A play tells you what the actors say and do to help the audience understand the story.

content.text: scenes

Props for Scene 2: party decorations, snacks, a comic book, Jana's backpack, and the same sketchbook as in Scene 1

content.text: Scene 1
Scene 1
(Setting: the kitchen. JANA is chopping carrots as AUNTIE TIMIKA stirs the pot.)
AUNTIE TIMIKA: How's your comic book coming along? Do you have a new superhero?
JANA: Actually, I came up with three superheroes! They're based on some kids in my class.
AUNTIE TIMIKA: Really? New friends?
(JANA picks up her sketchbook from the table to show AUNTIE TIMIKA.)

JANA: (with an embarrassed laugh) Well, not exactly friends, since I don't have the guts to actually talk to any of them. But they're really cool. This is Super Keisha. Her superpower is having an amazing singing voice. And this is Super Hal, whose superpower is being an awesome dancer. Super Tessa tells great jokes.
AUNTIE TIMIKA: (studying the pictures) These are great! You should put yourself in the story, too.
JANA: (frowning) Yeah, no. I have exactly zero superpowers.
AUNTIE TIMIKA: That's not—
(JANA's phone rings. She looks at the screen, eyebrows scrunched.)
JANA: Strange. It's this new boy, Rupert. Ms. Barrington made us study partners, but we never call each other.
AUNTIE TIMIKA: Well, he's calling now. Answer it!
JANA: (into the phone) Uh…hi? Well…sure, I…guess. Uh…okay, bye.
(JANA ends the call, her expression stunned.)
AUNTIE TIMIKA: Well?
JANA: (anxiously) He invited me to his birthday party, and I said yes. But only because I felt stuck. Ugh! I never know what to say at parties.
AUNTIE TIMIKA: If you said yes, you need to show up. Who knows? Maybe you'll have fun.
JANA: I seriously doubt it.
Scene 2
Scene 2

(Setting: a backyard, decorated for a birthday party. KEISHA, HAL, TESSA, and RUPERT are at the table eating snacks, laughing, and talking. JANA sits at the same table but is off to the side, looking through her sketchbook.)
RUPERT: I'm telling you, I've read Secrets of the Powdery Forest like ten times. Princess Fangs bites Swan Man, and he loses the power of flight. Don't you remember?
(JANA perks up, closing her sketchbook.)
TESSA: Nope, because it's Leaf Girl who lost the power of flight. Not Swan Man.
(JANA opens her mouth to speak, but KEISHA talks first.)
KEISHA: They both lost the power of flight.
(JANA opens her mouth again, but HAL talks first.)
HAL: Nobody lost the power of flight! They—

JANA: (blurting) Actually, Princess Fangs bit Swan Man in Night Cave. That's when he lost the power of flight. Princess Fangs almost bit Leaf Girl in Terrible Twilight, but Uncle Wind stopped her. Look, I drew pictures of it.
(JANA opens her sketchbook to show the others.)
RUPERT: (studying the pictures and laughing) She's right. We're all busted.
KEISHA: I remember these scenes now. Wow, you can really draw!
(The others nod.)
KEISHA: Can we see more?
JANA: Uh, I guess… (She turns the page, then freezes in alarm.) Wait, not this one—
RUPERT: Is that Hal?
Hal: (leaning in) Whoa! I'm a dancing superhero!
KEISHA: Am I in there?
TESSA: Am I?
JANA: (turning the page uncertainly) Yeah. I hope you don't mind.
KEISHA: Hey, I'm a singing superhero!
TESSA: And I'm a performing superhero. These are amazing.
RUPERT: Can you do me as a basketball superhero?
(JANA nods, smiling.)
RUPERT: Is your picture in here?
JANA: Me? No way.
KEISHA: Are you kidding? You should draw yourself as a comic artist superhero.
HAL: You could sell these!
TESSA: Definitely. Why'd you keep your comics a secret?
JANA: (grinning, pleased by the compliments) I don't know. Maybe I just…needed a superhero shove.
What do you learn about Jana from this dialogue?

Jana has trouble figuring out how to use her cell phone.

elements.text: Jana is off to the side by herself looking at her sketchbook.
When she hears the kids talk about comics, she perks up and puts the sketchbook away.
As the discussion continues, she attempts to participate.
As the others continue to get the facts wrong about the story, Jana blurts out the correct information.

contents.text: In Scene 1, Jana says that she doesn't feel brave enough to talk to the other kids. She also says she doesn't know what to say to people at parties. In Scene 2, instead of chatting with the others, she looks at her sketchbook away from the other kids. But when she notices that they are discussing comics, her attitude changes, and she joins in.
So, you can guess that the kids' discussion of comics helps Jana overcome her shyness.

elements.text: Scene 1: a dusty bus stop along an empty highway in a California farming town, 1944. There is a rusty metal bench. It is noontime, and the sun is glaring down.

elements.text: Prop for Scene 2: a shoebox filled with "Savage Cards"

content.text: Scene 1
Scene 1
(Setting: the front yard. ALEXA and ISAAC are in their tree house. LIAM is walking by on the sidewalk.)
ALEXA: (hissing) Beware! Alert! Alert!
(LIAM stops and looks around.)
ISAAC: (in a loud whisper) Up here, Liam!
LIAM: (looks up) Oh! Hi, guys. Why are you whispering at me?
ALEXA: Shhhh! It will hear you!
LIAM: (looking around) What will hear me?
ISAAC: (lowering the ladder) Come up and we'll tell you. Quick!
(LIAM runs through the gate into the yard. He quickly climbs the ladder, looking over his shoulder. ALEXA pulls up the ladder.)
ALEXA: Now you're safe.
LIAM: Safe from what?
ISAAC: The monster.
LIAM: A monster? Here? In our neighborhood?
(ALEXA and ISAAC nod seriously.)
ALEXA: It's a real menace.
ISAAC: That means it causes quite a bit of trouble.
LIAM: H-how?
ALEXA: (sighing) For one thing, the monster destroys stuff, while laughing in this creepy way.
ISAAC: And when it gets mad, it makes the loudest sound you've ever heard. Like a fire alarm, mixed with… (He looks to ALEXA for help.)
ALEXA: Mixed with thunder.
ISAAC: The sound could burst your eardrum.
ALEXA: Also, it slobbers. Goo is always dripping from its mouth. Always!
ISAAC: Sometimes the monster smells very (shivering)…very bad.
ALEXA: Very bad.
ISAAC: And the worst part? If you aren't paying attention (shuddering), it sits on you.
LIAM: (whispering) Seriously?
ALEXA and ISAAC: Seriously!
LIAM: (peeking out of the tree house) Where is it?
ALEXA: Napping. But it'll wake up soon.
Scene 2
Scene 2
(Setting: the same front yard, ten minutes later. A loud screech is heard offstage. LIAM jumps. ALEXA and ISAAC shudder.)
LIAM: (whispering) Is that the monster?
(ALEXA and ISAAC nod.)
ALEXA: It's coming.
(POPPY toddles into the yard wearing a diaper and a shirt. Dried food is all over her face.)
ALEXA and ISAAC: The monster!
LIAM: (crossing his arms and rolling his eyes) That's Poppy. Your sister.
ALEXA: Exactly.
ISAAC: Did you hear her monster screech?
ALEXA: Do you see that goo all over her face?
LIAM: (wrinkling his nose) That goo is kind of gross.
ALEXA: (jumping up and pointing) Isaac! You left your Savage Cards in the yard! The monster is going for them!
(POPPY is happily toddling toward the shoebox on the ground.)
ISAAC: Lower the ladder! Hurry!
(ALEXA lowers the ladder, and ISAAC quickly climbs down. He races toward the cards, but POPPY gets there first. She opens the box and flings the cards around her, giggling.)
ISAAC: Poppy, no!
ALEXA: (covering her eyes) I can't watch.
(ISAAC grabs the box, but POPPY clutches it and screams. Finally, ISAAC tugs it away, falling backward onto the grass. POPPY sits on him, giggling. Drool drips from her mouth onto his face.)
ISAAC: Help! Get her off me! She smells terrible!
(DAD enters the yard.)
DAD: Isaac, quiet down! Please! She's one. She's just trying to play with you, and you know it. (DAD scoops up POPPY and tickles her.) Ready for a diaper change, little monster?
ISAAC: (still sprawled in the grass) That was close. The monster almost destroyed me!
(LIAM and ALEXA burst out laughing.)
LIAM: I see what you guys mean.
ALEXA: Isaac, come back up, where it's safe.
LIAM: And bring your Savage Cards. We'll help you wipe off the goo.

content.text: play

pieces.text: is a story that is written so it can be performed for an audience. A play tells you what the actors say and do to help the audience understand the story.
Plays are often divided into different

content.text: scenes

pieces.text: , or parts of the play. When a new scene starts, that shows you that either time has passed or the setting has changed.

contents.text: In Scene 1, Alexa and Isaac tell Liam that a monster is coming, and they describe the monster.

In Scene 2, Alexa and Isaac's little sister Poppy enters, and she fits the description of the monster they had described. Liam realizes that Alexa and Isaac had been talking about Poppy as if she were a monster.
So, the play is about two kids who tell their friend about a terrible monster, and the friend waits to see what the monster is.

passage.text: Have you ever stopped to think about why your favorite foods taste so good? If you look closely at your tongue in a mirror, you will notice that it's completely covered in tiny bumps. Your taste buds can be found inside those bumps. They allow you to experience the sweet flavor of a fresh chocolate chip cookie or the sour taste of a lemon.

However, the taste buds also get some help from your nose. While you're chewing, the smell of the food travels up your nose. Your brain pairs the information from your taste buds with the information from your nose to determine the flavor. If your nose is stuffy, you might notice that foods do not taste as good. That's because when your nose is stuffed, it can't receive the smell of the food you're chewing. Therefore, your nose can't send that information to your brain. Without smell, your taste buds can tell your brain a little about what you're eating, such as whether it's sweet or bitter, but they cannot give the whole picture.

Children are born with around ten thousand taste buds. Every week or so, when they start to wear out, they are replaced by new taste buds. Also, taste buds will grow back after getting damaged, and their recovery time is quick. For example, if you burn your tongue on hot chocolate, your taste buds will be up and working again in a few short days. However, as we get older, some of our taste buds are not replaced. The number of taste buds might drop down to between two thousand and five thousand for an older person. At the same time, older people's sense of smell decreases. Without a strong sense of smell, it is more difficult for the brain to recognize flavors. This explains why tastes can change over time.

The more taste buds you have, the stronger the flavors you can experience. People with over ten thousand taste buds are called supertasters, and their experience of flavors is more intense. Children, who have a lot of taste buds, often taste flavors more strongly, too. This is one reason why some children prefer not to eat certain foods. The slightly bitter flavor of asparagus tastes fine to most adults, but the bitterness is much stronger to children since they have a greater number of taste buds.

Besides giving foods their flavor, taste buds have another important job: to help keep us safe. Foods that might be dangerous often taste bitter or sour, which means that our sense of taste helps us test the foods we eat and may warn us if something is unsafe.

passage.text: If you have ever collected seashells, you know that they come in a wide range of shapes and colors. But why is that? Many things help decide a shell's appearance, including where it is formed and how it is used for protection.

To understand a shell's appearance, it's important to first understand what shells are. Most seashells are the exoskeletons of different kinds of mollusks, such as snails, clams, and oysters. An exoskeleton is an animal's hard outer covering. As a mollusk grows, it uses chemicals from the sea to produce a compound of calcium, which becomes the hard exoskeleton. The exoskeleton shields the mollusk's soft, slimy body. When the mollusk dies, its soft body rots away or is eaten by a predator. Its exoskeleton may wash to the shore, where people call it a seashell.

A seashell's appearance is affected by its environment. For example, warmer waters tend to produce more colorful seashells. This is partly because warm waters contain more food sources for mollusks. The foods contain different pigments, substances that give them their color. Since mollusks in warmer waters eat foods with many different pigments, they create more colorful exoskeletons. Mollusks found in colder waters have a more limited food supply. Therefore, their exoskeletons tend to be darker and more uniform in color.

The main role of a mollusk's exoskeleton is to protect the mollusk inside. So, a shell's thickness and shape depend on how it is used for protection. Thin shells are lighter than thick shells. Thus, mollusks that avoid predators by swimming away often have thin shells. The shell's light weight allows the mollusk to move around more easily. To make up for their thinness, these shells often have spikes and ridges to give them more strength. In addition, the spikes and ridges give the mollusk extra protection against predators. Mollusks that burrow underground, like clams, also have thin shells so they can dig quickly. These mollusks have smooth shells, however, since predators cannot easily get to them underground. Finally, some mollusks form thick, heavy shells to deter predators. These heavy shells are difficult for predators to break through, and they also help anchor the mollusks to surfaces like rocks and mud.

A seashell's appearance is affected by its environment. For example, warmer waters tend to produce more colorful seashells. This is partly because warm waters contain more food sources for mollusks. The foods contain different pigments, substances that give them their color. Since mollusks in warmer waters eat foods with many different pigments, they create more colorful exoskeletons. Mollusks found in colder waters have a more limited food supply. Therefore, their exoskeletons tend to be darker and more uniform in color.

The main role of a mollusk's exoskeleton is to protect the mollusk inside. So, a shell's thickness and shape depend on how it is used for protection. Thin shells are lighter than thick shells. Thus, mollusks that avoid predators by swimming away often have thin shells. The shell's light weight allows the mollusk to move around more easily. To make up for their thinness, these shells often have spikes and ridges to give them more strength. In addition, the spikes and ridges give the mollusk extra protection against predators. Mollusks that burrow underground, like clams, also have thin shells so they can dig quickly. These mollusks have smooth shells, however, since predators cannot easily get to them underground. Finally, some mollusks form thick, heavy shells to deter predators. These heavy shells are difficult for predators to break through, and they also help anchor the mollusks to surfaces like rocks and mud.

Every seashell was once a mollusk's home. Each seashell was built differently in order to suit the creature living inside. These animals create shells that give them the best chance of living safely in their environments.

passage.text: Bacteria are bad, right? Aren't bacteria the tiny little "germs" that make us sick? We have antibacterial soaps and cleaning products to kill bacteria, and we have antibiotic medicines to stop infections caused by bacteria. People and bacteria don't get along, right? Well, the truth isn't that simple. Actually, most bacteria are our friends. We could not live without these tiny living organisms.

It's a good thing that most bacteria are not the enemy—because they are everywhere. They are in the soil, the air, the water, and in and on every part of our bodies. Some bacteria can even survive in extreme habitats, such as deep underground or in boiling hot springs. Bacteria are the smallest known living things on the planet, with about ten thousand species discovered so far.

Each person's body has trillions of bacteria. In our digestive systems, bacteria help break down the food we eat so our bodies can use the nutrients and get rid of the waste. Some bacteria in our bodies likely produce important nutrients, such as vitamin K, themselves. One of the most important jobs for our bodies' good bacteria is to keep the bad bacteria out. Good bacteria help keep our bodies strong and ready to fight off diseases caused by bad bacteria.

Bacteria are not only important for our bodies. They are important for the environment, too. Bacteria in soil break down dead plant and animal materials. This cleans things up, and it also fertilizes the soil to help new plants grow. Bacteria have even been used to break down garbage stored in landfills and oil that pollutes water after oil spills. Researchers have even discovered bacteria that feed on plastic, one of the hardest types of garbage to break down.

While there are many benefits of bacteria, some scary diseases can be caused by bad bacteria. For example, the bubonic plague, also known as the Black Death, killed millions of people in the fourteenth century. Dangerous, contagious diseases like these can quickly spread to others, making large numbers of people sick at once. Thankfully, most diseases today that are caused by bacteria can be treated with antibiotics. However, antibiotics cannot tell the difference between good and bad bacteria. So, they kill off good bacteria along with the bad. At times, some bad bacteria can survive the antibiotics and become even stronger. So, doctors try to use antibiotics only when they are truly needed to fight off certain bacterial infections.

The benefits of bacteria in our world are many and growing. While it is true that we have to be careful about spreading bad bacteria, there are many more good bacteria that are our friends. They're like a microscopic army fighting alongside us to make our bodies and our world healthier.

passage.text: Bacteria are bad, right? Aren't bacteria the tiny little "germs" that make us sick? We have antibacterial soaps and cleaning products to kill bacteria, and we have antibiotic medicines to stop infections caused by bacteria. People and bacteria don't get along, right? Well, the truth isn't that simple. Actually, most bacteria are our friends. We could not live without these tiny living organisms.

It's a good thing that most bacteria are not the enemy—because they are everywhere. They are in the soil, the air, the water, and in and on every part of our bodies. Some bacteria can even survive in extreme habitats, such as deep underground or in boiling hot springs. Bacteria are the smallest known living things on the planet, with about ten thousand species discovered so far.

Each person's body has trillions of bacteria. In our digestive systems, bacteria help break down the food we eat so our bodies can use the nutrients and get rid of the waste. Some bacteria in our bodies likely produce important nutrients, such as vitamin K, themselves. One of the most important jobs for our bodies' good bacteria is to keep the bad bacteria out. Good bacteria help keep our bodies strong and ready to fight off diseases caused by bad bacteria.

Bacteria are not only important for our bodies. They are important for the environment, too. Bacteria in soil break down dead plant and animal materials. This cleans things up, and it also fertilizes the soil to help new plants grow. Bacteria have even been used to break down garbage stored in landfills and oil that pollutes water after oil spills. Researchers have even discovered bacteria that feed on plastic, one of the hardest types of garbage to break down.

While there are many benefits of bacteria, some scary diseases can be caused by bad bacteria. For example, the bubonic plague, also known as the Black Death, killed millions of people in the fourteenth century. Dangerous, contagious diseases like these can quickly spread to others, making large numbers of people sick at once. Thankfully, most diseases today that are caused by bacteria can be treated with antibiotics. However, antibiotics cannot tell the difference between good and bad bacteria. So, they kill off good bacteria along with the bad. At times, some bad bacteria can survive the antibiotics and become even stronger. So, doctors try to use antibiotics only when they are truly needed to fight off certain bacterial infections.

The benefits of bacteria in our world are many and growing. While it is true that we have to be careful about spreading bad bacteria, there are many more good bacteria that are our friends. They're like a microscopic army fighting alongside us to make our bodies and our world healthier.

passage.text: Sir Isaac Newton was one of history's greatest thinkers. Born in England in 1643, Newton focused his early studies on science. He made discoveries about the science of color and the movements of planets. In 1668, he designed and built a new type of telescope. It was his first big success in science. Newton's most lasting achievement, however, would be a set of three books.

Newton published these books in 1687, after eighteen months of intense writing and study. The original books were written in Latin and were together called Principia. The books were later translated into English. Principia described Newton's laws of motion. These laws explained the movement of objects on Earth and throughout the universe. Newton's laws of motion also helped him develop a theory of gravity, which he also described in Principia. This theory explained how the sun's gravity keeps the planets in orbit and how Earth's gravity keeps the moon in orbit. The laws also allowed Newton to figure out the mass of each planet and even why Earth's oceans have tides.

Edmond Halley, a friend of Newton's and a famous scientist in his own right, helped with the books. Halley edited Principia and offered support and encouragement. When it was finished, the Royal Society, an important group of scientists, agreed to publish Newton's books. However, the society then spent all of its money on a book about the history of fishes and could not afford to publish Newton's work. This was disappointing, but Newton's friend Halley saved Principia by paying for the books to be printed himself.

Though Principia was published more than three hundred years ago, it is still considered one of the greatest scientific works ever printed. Some even consider it one of the greatest works ever published on any subject. The British astronaut Tim Peake called Newton "Britain's greatest scientist." In 2014, Peake honored Newton by choosing the name Principia for his mission to the International Space Station. In December 2016, a copy of Principia dating back to its first printing sold for $3.7 million! As a result, it set a record as the most expensive printed science book ever sold at an auction.

Without a doubt, Principia has stood the test of time. Newton's Principia is still studied by scientists today, and their sustained interest shows the importance of Newton's work. It is not likely to be forgotten anytime soon.

passage.text: Sir Isaac Newton was one of history's greatest thinkers. Born in England in 1643, Newton focused his early studies on science. He made discoveries about the science of color and the movements of planets. In 1668, he designed and built a new type of telescope. It was his first big success in science. Newton's most lasting achievement, however, would be a set of three books.

Newton published these books in 1687, after eighteen months of intense writing and study. The original books were written in Latin and were together called Principia. The books were later translated into English. Principia described Newton's laws of motion. These laws explained the movement of objects on Earth and throughout the universe. Newton's laws of motion also helped him develop a theory of gravity, which he also described in Principia. This theory explained how the sun's gravity keeps the planets in orbit and how Earth's gravity keeps the moon in orbit. The laws also allowed Newton to figure out the mass of each planet and even why Earth's oceans have tides.

Edmond Halley, a friend of Newton's and a famous scientist in his own right, helped with the books. Halley edited Principia and offered support and encouragement. When it was finished, the Royal Society, an important group of scientists, agreed to publish Newton's books. However, the society then spent all of its money on a book about the history of fishes and could not afford to publish Newton's work. This was disappointing, but Newton's friend Halley saved Principia by paying for the books to be printed himself.

Though Principia was published more than three hundred years ago, it is still considered one of the greatest scientific works ever printed. Some even consider it one of the greatest works ever published on any subject. The British astronaut Tim Peake called Newton "Britain's greatest scientist." In 2014, Peake honored Newton by choosing the name Principia for his mission to the International Space Station. In December 2016, a copy of Principia dating back to its first printing sold for $3.7 million! As a result, it set a record as the most expensive printed science book ever sold at an auction.

Without a doubt, Principia has stood the test of time. Newton's Principia is still studied by scientists today, and their sustained interest shows the importance of Newton's work. It is not likely to be forgotten anytime soon.

passage.text: It is hard to imagine anything more frightening than a blazing forest fire, crackling loudly as it burns through everything in its path. Forest fires can destroy plants, animal homes, and food sources for the creatures that live within the forest. However, when forest fires begin naturally and are controlled quickly, there are hidden benefits. These fires play an important role in the cycle of forest life.

Many forest fires are caused by humans, but some occur naturally. Lightning strikes are the most common way that Mother Nature causes forest fires. Fire can be nature's way of helping the forest thrive. A forest fire often clears out weeds, harmful insects, and plants that have diseases. Fire also eliminates underbrush crowding the forest floor. Old rotting logs and dead leaves are burned up, so their nutrients are broken down and returned to the soil as ash. The extra nutrients in the soil after a fire help to create a more fertile area for new plants to grow.

The highest area in a large forest is called the canopy. From above, the leafy canopy looks like a large green cover over the forest. This cover can block out the sun. However, a fire helps open up the forest canopy. After the thick leaves are partly burned away, sunlight can reach smaller, younger trees below. With low-growing underbrush and dead matter also burned away, sunlight can reach all the way down to the forest floor. After the fire ends, the sunlight helps young plants to sprout and grow.

Within the forest are moist areas that are naturally protected from burning. Therefore, even the largest fires do not usually destroy the entire forest. The trees that make it through the fire create seeds to regrow the forest. Some trees even have cones that only open and release their seeds when heated by fire. The new seeds, joined with the especially fertile soil and the extra sunlight, help to bring new life to the forest.

Besides allowing new plants to thrive, the open areas created after a controlled fire provide benefits for wildlife. New growth, like grasses, herbs, and shrubs, provide food and shelter for a wide range of animals. In addition, burned trees actually provide habitats for certain species of birds and small mammals. The loss caused by a forest fire can be severe, but naturally occurring fires that are controlled serve a necessary purpose.

passage.text: It is hard to imagine anything more frightening than a blazing forest fire, crackling loudly as it burns through everything in its path. Forest fires can destroy plants, animal homes, and food sources for the creatures that live within the forest. However, when forest fires begin naturally and are controlled quickly, there are hidden benefits. These fires play an important role in the cycle of forest life.

Many forest fires are caused by humans, but some occur naturally. Lightning strikes are the most common way that Mother Nature causes forest fires. Fire can be nature's way of helping the forest thrive. A forest fire often clears out weeds, harmful insects, and plants that have diseases. Fire also eliminates underbrush crowding the forest floor. Old rotting logs and dead leaves are burned up, so their nutrients are broken down and returned to the soil as ash. The extra nutrients in the soil after a fire help to create a more fertile area for new plants to grow.

The highest area in a large forest is called the canopy. From above, the leafy canopy looks like a large green cover over the forest. This cover can block out the sun. However, a fire helps open up the forest canopy. After the thick leaves are partly burned away, sunlight can reach smaller, younger trees below. With low-growing underbrush and dead matter also burned away, sunlight can reach all the way down to the forest floor. After the fire ends, the sunlight helps young plants to sprout and grow.

Within the forest are moist areas that are naturally protected from burning. Therefore, even the largest fires do not usually destroy the entire forest. The trees that make it through the fire create seeds to regrow the forest. Some trees even have cones that only open and release their seeds when heated by fire. The new seeds, joined with the especially fertile soil and the extra sunlight, help to bring new life to the forest.

Besides allowing new plants to thrive, the open areas created after a controlled fire provide benefits for wildlife. New growth, like grasses, herbs, and shrubs, provide food and shelter for a wide range of animals. In addition, burned trees actually provide habitats for certain species of birds and small mammals. The loss caused by a forest fire can be severe, but naturally occurring fires that are controlled serve a necessary purpose.
